cards.text: We're still inside Ezekiel's vision, friend. Ezekiel, a prophet living in exile, has been following a man who looks like bronze, carrying a measuring rod, while the man measures the temple's walls, gates and courts (Ezekiel 40:1-3). Now the man brings him into the outer sanctuary and measures it: forty cubits long and twenty cubits wide.

cards.question: From the outer sanctuary, the man keeps going deeper into the temple. He goes into the ___ sanctuary.
By the inner sanctuary, the man measures a room twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. Then he tells Ezekiel what this room is. What does he call it?

cards.text: Then that measuring rod gets BUSY: side rooms in three levels of thirty rooms each, a building out back, and the whole temple a hundred cubits long. I stamp cookies for a living, friend, and I'd have lost count by the second level.
Inside, the walls are paneled with wood and carved all around with cherubim and palm trees. Each cherub has two faces, a man's and a young lion's, and here I am with ONE face that's mostly mustache.

cards.question: Then Ezekiel sees an altar made of wood, three cubits high. The man tells him what it is. What does he call it?

answers.text: The table that is before the LORD
The mercy seat of the LORD

cards.text: Both sanctuaries have double doors, and the outer sanctuary's doors are carved with cherubim and palm trees, just like the walls. Even the DOORS are dressed up, friend, and the best decoration on my bakery door is a floury mustache print.

Then the man leads Ezekiel north into the outer court, to a three-story building of chambers, with a matching set on the south side, and the man finally explains what these chambers are FOR. FINALLY! I've been holding that question in since the side rooms.

cards.question: The man says these north and south chambers are the holy chambers where the ___ who approach the LORD will eat the most holy offerings.
The man says the most holy offerings are placed in these chambers because the place is holy.

cards.text: Then the man gives a rule about what the priests WEAR once they've gone into the holy area. Turns out there's a dress code, friend, and it's stricter than my apron.

cards.question: Once priests have entered the holy area, they can walk out into the outer court wearing the garments they minister in.
Why must the priests leave their ministering garments behind before going out to the outer court?

answers.text: Because those garments belong to the high priest

cards.question: The priests put on other clothes before they approach the places that are for the ___.
When the man finishes measuring the inside of the temple area, he leads Ezekiel out by the gate that faces east.

cards.text: Then he measures all four sides with his rod: east, five hundred cubits; north, five hundred; south, five hundred; west, FIVE HUNDRED. Four for four, and back in my worn-out days I couldn't stamp two cookies the same size.

cards.question: The whole area is five hundred cubits on every side, with a wall all the way around it. What is that wall for?

answers.text: To separate the holy from the common
To keep enemy armies from getting in
To mark where the city's edge begins

cards.text: And that's where the measuring rod rests for now, friend. This temple tour isn't over, and trust me, my apron's already on for whatever comes next.

findings.problem: Card 1 says the man has been measuring the temple's walls, gates and courts, and cites Ezekiel 40:1-3. Those verses only introduce the man with the measuring rod. The measuring of the walls, gates and courts happens in Ezekiel 40:5-49, so the reference does not cover the fact.

rule.text: **References.** Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The setup says the man 'keeps going deeper into the temple.' That rules out 'upper' and 'eastern' and points straight to 'inner,' so the line gives the answer away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: Card 8 is three sentences ('Then the man leads... FOR.' / 'FINALLY!' / 'I've been holding...'). It also packs four beats into one card: going north into the outer court, the three-story building of chambers, the matching chambers on the south, and the man explaining their purpose.

rule.text: **Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.** ... Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The joke 'I've been holding that question in since the side rooms' ties the man's explanation to the side rooms of 41:5-11. But the explanation in 42:13 is about the north and south chambers, not the side rooms. The callback makes the wrong connection and leaves a reader asking 'huh?'

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: 'It's stricter than my apron' doesn't click. An apron isn't a dress code, so the comparison has no shared action and needs explaining.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action. ... It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining. If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: Almost the whole passage is building plans: measurements, side rooms, carvings, doors and chambers. The walkthrough spreads the building detail over four separate summary story cards (4, 5, 7, 8) and asks choice cards on building details such as the inner sanctuary (card 2) and the east gate (card 15). The docs say a long stretch gets one summary card and never a choice card. They don't say what to do when nearly the entire passage is one long stretch, apart from the man's spoken lines (41:4, 41:22, 42:13-14).
findings.question: When a passage is almost entirely a building plan, should it still get only one summary story card, with choice cards limited to what the man says (41:4, 41:22, 42:13-14) and the purpose of the wall (42:20)? Or may the building detail be split into several summary cards, with choice cards on details like the inner sanctuary and the east gate?
